transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-08
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Vega (Nimbus ML Eng), Mei Chen (Nimbus Infra), Ravi Patel (Nimbus CTO)
---
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to focus today on squeezing more throughput out of your workload without blowing up latency tails. priya will walk through scheduler knobs and some live numbers.
[00:18] Priya: yeah hi hi, thanks, so quick agenda, continuous batching behavior, max_num_seqs and per-worker seq caps, token limits and how they affect batching, kv cache warmup and steady-state hit rates, and brief note on quantization effects. then we'll map to a pilot.
[00:32] Carlos: sounds good, im mostly interested because our downstream cost is spiking when we batch naively.
[00:40] Priya: right, ok quick background, our runtime uses continuous batching so requests are queued and assembled into batches over a short window. two knobs matter a lot: max_batch_size and max_num_seqs. max_batch_size is tokens-per-batch soft cap and max_num_seqs limits how many concurrent sequences we put in a single decode step.
[00:58] Mei: can you say 'sequences' again? like, is that per request or per chunk?
[01:05] Priya: yep per incoming logical request—if you stream tokens we count the active sequences being decoded. so a single request with temperature sampling still counts as one seq unless you do n-best sampling.
[01:18] Ravi: we've set a 1s accumulation window currently and a max_batch_size of 512, but we see long tails at p95.
[01:26] Priya: accumulation window is a trade: longer window -> bigger batches -> better throughput/cost, but you increase head latency. continuous batching tries to be adaptive: if idle, it will flush early. key trick: you can use max_num_seqs to avoid pathological head-of-line blocking.
[01:44] Jordan: one way customers do this is lower the accumulation window to 100-150ms and raise max_num_seqs so that more short requests group across workers rather than saturating one worker with long seqs.
[01:59] Carlos: our distribution: 70% short prompts (<=64 tokens), 20% medium (65-256), 10% long (>256). what's the recommended max_num_seqs for that?
[02:12] Priya: for that distribution I'd start with max_num_seqs=48 on V100-equivalent workers or 64 on A100-equivalent; it's heuristic—what matters is average tokens-in-flight. if you set max_num_seqs too high on older hardware you can saturate memory and get longer decode times per step.
[02:30] Mei: memory? is that the KV cache blowing up?
[02:33] Priya: yes, kv cache size scales with seq length * batch_size. so large max_num_seqs with many long sequences increases kv memory. recommended to set a ceiling on max_tokens_per_worker too (we call it max_tokens_in_flight in our config).
[02:49] Ravi: do you have an example config you recommend?
[02:52] Priya: i'll share a doc but quick baseline: accumulation_window_ms=120, max_batch_size_tokens=1024, max_num_seqs=48 (A100:64), max_tokens_in_flight=65536, idle_batch_timeout_ms=30. those are starting points.
[03:12] Carlos: idle_batch_timeout?
[03:14] Priya: it's the micro-flush threshold—if a partial batch hasn't filled but no new request arrives for that timeout, flush to avoid latency stalling. 20-50ms usually.
[03:23] [00:03:30] Speaker 1 (transcript engine): note: some terms may be transcribed incorrectly, e.g., 'kay vee cache' = KV cache.
[03:36] Carlos: interesting, ok, how about tail latency problems when we have a mix of very long and very short sequences?
[03:43] Priya: two complementary strategies: 1) request routing by seq length—short requests get dispatched to low-latency queues/workers with lower max_num_seqs and smaller accumulation windows; long requests go to throughput-optimized workers. 2) preemptive quota: limit how many long seqs can occupy the same worker concurrently.
[04:00] Mei: does Redwood runtime support automatic routing by estimated tokens?
[04:04] Priya: yes, you can set request predicates (e.g., estimated_tokens>256) that route to a different pool. We also have an autoscaling policy per pool.
[04:12] Jordan: another lever is prefix caching—if many requests share a common prompt prefix, KV cache hits reduce effective per-token work and improve throughput. but cache warmup matters.
[04:23] Carlos: our prompts have a 30-token system + variable user prompt—so prefix caching should help. how long to warm?
[04:29] Priya: depends on cache TTL and request rate; in steady state with 70% short prompts you might hit warm state in 1-2 minutes. however, cold starts after a deployment will need a warmup run.
[04:40] Ravi: about quantization—we're exploring q4_0 and int8—what's the impact on throughput and latency?
[04:47] Priya: quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput since compute kernels are faster, but impact varies by model. q4_0 often reduces memory by ~2-3x and increases throughput ~20-40% on decoder steps. caveat: some models show quality regressions in edge cases. we recommend validating with your eval set.
[05:04] Mei: does quantization change KV cache behavior?
[05:07] Priya: not directly—the cache stores hidden states; quantized models may use different kernel layouts but cache size in bytes is affected by precision. e.g., int8 cache will be smaller in memory footprint, enabling higher max_num_seqs.
[05:20] Carlos: you mentioned scheduler knobs—can you list the full set we should tune?
[05:24] Priya: sure: accumulation_window_ms, idle_batch_timeout_ms, max_batch_size_tokens, max_num_seqs, max_tokens_in_flight (per-worker cap), per-request token_limit, request routing predicates, warmup_preheat (optional to pre-populate KV cache), and quantization_profile selection.
[05:44] [00:06:00] Jordan: also watch for token_limit per request: if customers set a high per-request token_limit (like 8192) and have many long requests, it inflates batch memory. configure a reasonable per-request cap or route long requests.
[05:58] Ravi: about monitoring—what metrics should we track during tuning?
[06:02] Priya: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, tokens-per-second per-worker, avg batch size (seqs and tokens), KV cache hit ratio, memory utilization per GPU, OOM events, and scheduling queue length. Redwood console emits token-level cost breakdowns too.
[06:18] Carlos: is there an automated advisor to recommend knobs?
[06:21] Priya: Redwood Optimize has recommendations, but for complex mixes we still do hand-tuned pilots. we'll share a spreadsheet template for analysis.
[06:29] Mei: ok, pilot plan—how should we run the pilot?
[06:32] Priya: two phases: 1) Replay: run a 1-hour replay of production traces against a Dedicated pool sized similarly to your expected capacity; measure throughput and tail latency. 2) Stress: synthetic ramp to 2-3x expected qps to validate autoscaling and fallback. We'll instrument metrics and adjust knobs iteratively.
[06:50] Carlos: what's the expected cost delta when increasing max_num_seqs?
[06:54] Priya: cost per token should go down because batching efficiency improves, but GPU memory pressure may require larger instances or lower parallelism which can raise hourly spend. net effect usually tilts toward cost savings for token-heavy workloads; exact numbers depend. we'll quantify in the pilot.
[07:10] Ravi: VPC/on-prem note: we prefer private deployment due to data residency. do any of these knobs behave differently on Private?
[07:17] Priya: same runtime, same knobs. differences are operational: networking latency inside your VPC can affect accumulation behavior if your ingress is throttled. also, if you use on-prem GPUs with less memory, recommended max_num_seqs will be lower.
[07:31] Mei: are there any known scheduler bugs we should watch for?
[07:34] Priya: nothing major in the current release, but corner cases with extremely bursty traffic (millisecond spikes) can cause temporary head-of-line blocking; we log those as backpressure events. We'll enable verbose scheduler traces for the pilot.
[07:47] [00:07:50] Speaker 2 (transcriber): transcription note: timestamps approximate.
[07:52] Carlos: can you demo a quick sim of increasing max_num_seqs and how batch composition changes?
[07:57] Priya: sure, i'll share screen and a simple ascii sim—(brief pause while sharing)
[08:10] Priya: ok imagine 10 incoming short reqs (10x64 tokens) and 2 long reqs (2x512). with max_num_seqs=16, you might pack 10 shorts + 2 longs into one big batch, kv size spikes. with max_num_seqs=48 and per-worker token cap, the runtime will spread sequences across multiple decode partitions, improving throughput but raising per-step compute.
[08:39] Carlos: any gotchas when you use streaming responses?
[08:42] Priya: streaming keeps seqs active longer in memory which reduces batch turnover; so for streaming-heavy workloads, you want lower max_num_seqs and smaller accumulation windows to keep latency good. alternatively route streaming to dedicated low-latency workers.
[08:59] Ravi: how do fallbacks work if a requested model variant isn't available during pilot?
[09:03] Jordan: we have automatic fallback policies—route to a compatible quantized variant or a region. For critical paths you can pin versions to avoid surprises.
[09:11] Mei: security question: if we use VPC + KMS, does Redwood need access to keys?
[09:16] Jordan: for Private deployments you keep KMS in your account and Redwood does not have key access. for Hosted, keys are managed by Redwood—there are options for bring-your-own-key (BYOK) with HSM integrations. we'll attach the security whitepaper.
[09:28] [00:09:40] Carlos: ok good. any notes on per-request token_limit enforcement? we sometimes see clients accidentally set enormous limits in the UI.
[09:36] Priya: you can enforce server-side per-user max_token_limit and reject or coerce requests. We support that at the route level.
[09:43] Carlos: nice.
[09:45] Priya: quick demo numbers from our lab cluster (A100): baseline continuous batching with defaults: 2000 tok/s per GPU, p95 latency 220ms. with tuned knobs (accumulation 120ms, max_num_seqs 64, quant q4_0) we saw 2600 tok/s and p95 down to 180ms on short prompts, but p99 occasionally rose when long seqs interleaved.
[10:09] Ravi: so p99 risk remains—how do we cap that?
[10:12] Priya: enforce routing by length + set per-pool SLOs and automatic fallback to smaller model variants under high queue depth. also use preemptive eviction policies for very long-running sequences if they violate SLOs.
[10:25] Jordan: ok time to align on deliverables—Priya will share the config doc and a spreadsheet. Carlos will provide traces. Mei will provision test infra. Jordan will set the pilot date.
[10:36] Carlos: one more operational question: how do we visualize batch composition in the console?
[10:40] Priya: per-route dashboard shows avg seqs-per-batch, tokens-per-batch, and batch size distribution histogram. we'll enable those on your account for the pilot.
[10:51] [00:11:00] Speaker 3 (system): link references: scheduler knobs doc (internal): https://redwood.internal/docs/scheduler-knobs.md ; pilot spreadsheet template: https://redwood.internal/templates/pilot-spreadsheet.xlsx
[11:05] Ravi: thanks everyone.
[11:08] Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts. Recap: share docs, provide traces, schedule pilot.
[11:15] Mei: ok. that works.
